\subsection{Preliminary Extension: Event Extraction}
\label{sec:wikievents}

We apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 roles, 27 entity types, 245 constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}) without modification.
Violations extend to EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and AC (argument constraint, analogous to DR).

%  exp_ids: ee_{qwen,llama,mistral}_wikievents_{unconstrained,grammar_only,constrained_v3}

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained EE produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV $>$85\%; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), with entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot process off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all models, which validates the tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE and SentencePiece.
Grammar-only eliminates EV but leaves RoV at 64--77\% and surfaces latent AC (8--14\%), consistent with DocRED's pattern (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); full S1 drives RoV to 0\%.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to semantically similar types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN).
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument structures increase entity reuse across slots.
Post-hoc filtering is impractical ($<$0.5\% arguments retained).
Unlike RE, EE shows measurable F1 gains: entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%, trigger F1 $+$1.5--1.8\,pp.

% exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning (preliminary).}
WikiEvents uses a 194/20/20 train/dev/test split~\cite{li2021document}; the 20-document test set is a dataset constraint, not a design choice.
LoRA + S1 eliminates RoV (Qwen 38.31\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 8.8\%\,$\to$\,0\%; bootstrap 95\% CI [0\%,\,0\%] and [0\%,\,1.73\%]) and reduces AC to $\leq$0.8\%, with argument F1 within $\pm$1.1\,pp; trigger F1 shows larger shifts ($-$5.4/$-$0.6\,pp) with wide confidence intervals at this sample size.
CF remains low under fine-tuning (0.77--1.18\%), consistent with RE composability results (\S\ref{sec:composition}, Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Constrained decoding does not further reduce EE CF because the semantic layer enforces per-event role-type compatibility but not cross-event entity type consensus, the same architectural limitation identified in RE (\S\ref{sec:composition}).

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.

\paragraph{Grammar-constrained decoding.}
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and Grammar-Aligned Decoding~\cite{park2024grammar} guarantee format validity via CFG-based token masking; JSONSchemaBench~\cite{jsonschemabench2025} benchmarks these systems.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} applies grammar constraints to IE tasks.
In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} enforce type constraints via incremental parsing, and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems into prefix automata.
These methods ensure syntactic or type-level validity but operate on static type declarations; IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, where constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation type.
OntoCoDec's grammar layer builds on XGrammar; its semantic layer extends constrained decoding from syntax to ontology-level type enforcement.

\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} encode ontology structure as Python dataclasses and train models to generate typed code;
REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, DeepStruct~\cite{wang2022deepstruct}, UIE~\cite{lu2022uie}, USM~\cite{lou2023usm}, and UniversalNER~\cite{zhou2024universalner} unify extraction via structured training, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
These methods internalize constraints through training; code-generation approaches such as GoLLIE achieve type compliance through format constraints (class names encode types) but with limited zero-shot relation coverage.
OntoCoDec enforces types at decoding time without retraining while preserving extraction capability.

\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
\citet{roth_yih_2004} first formulated hard type constraints for IE via integer linear programming; OntoCoDec achieves analogous enforcement within autoregressive decoding.
Post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} detects violations after generation and requires rejection or correction cycles.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025} combines constrained and unconstrained decoding for IE; SchemaRL~\cite{schema_rl2025} uses reinforcement learning to align generation with schema constraints; DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} accelerates constrained decoding via draft-conditioned generation.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, requires no constraint-specific training, and compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies.

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) guarantees JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning, with rates characterized by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\kappa}$) rather than schema or model scale.
% exp_ids: w5_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_qwen_docred_lora_constrained_eval, w5_llama_lora_scierc_constrained_eval, w5_llama_docred_lora_constrained_eval
Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), \textsc{OntoCoDec} eliminates DR violations with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; beam search ($k{=}4$) resolves the cross-field consistency (CF) trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (R-F1 44--46, 1.54$\times$ latency).
Under zero-shot decoding, DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.
The framework extends to event extraction without modification.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM across four models (8B--70B) and three tokenizer families.
\end{abstract}

\begin{abstract}
We present \textsc{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles Information Extraction (IE) ontologies into composable token-level decoding constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: a \emph{grammar layer} (context-free) guarantees JSON validity and vocabulary membership; a \emph{semantic layer} (prefix-decidable with state) enforces per-triple domain/range type constraints via a stateful entity registry, with grammar-first fallback when constraints conflict.
Without constraints, Large Language Model (LLM) based IE produces systematic domain/range (DR) violations that persist after fine-tuning, with rates characterized by \emph{constraint tightness} ($\bar{\kappa}$) rather than schema or model scale.

Composed with Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), \textsc{OntoCoDec} eliminates DR violations while maintaining or improving R-F1; beam search ($k{=}4$) resolves the cross-field consistency (CF) trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (R-F1 44--46, 1.54$\times$ latency).
Under zero-shot decoding, DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.
The framework extends to event extraction without modification.
\textsc{OntoCoDec} compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM across four models (8B--70B) and three tokenizer families.
\end{abstract}

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

We provide a detailed survey in Appendix~\ref{app:related_work}; here we position OntoCoDec along three axes.

\paragraph{Grammar-constrained decoding.}
XGrammar~\cite{dong2025xgrammar}, Outlines~\cite{willard2023outlines}, LMQL~\cite{beurer-kellner2023lmql}, SynCode~\cite{ugare2024syncode}, and Grammar-Aligned Decoding~\cite{park2024grammar} guarantee format validity via CFG-based token masking; JSONSchemaBench~\cite{jsonschemabench2025} benchmarks these systems.
GCD~\cite{geng2023gcd} applies grammar constraints to IE tasks.
In code generation, PICARD~\cite{scholak2021picard} and Synchromesh~\cite{synchromesh_iclr2022} enforce type constraints via incremental parsing, and \citet{pldi2025_type_constrained_codegen} compile full type systems into prefix automata.
These methods ensure syntactic or type-level validity but operate on static type declarations; IE requires a dynamic entity registry built during generation, where constraint targets depend on the co-occurring relation type.
OntoCoDec's grammar layer builds on XGrammar; its semantic layer extends constrained decoding from syntax to ontology-level type enforcement.

\paragraph{Schema-aware IE.}
GoLLIE~\cite{sainz2024gollie}, GUIDEX~\cite{guidex2025}, and KnowCoder~\cite{knowcoder_acl2024} encode ontology structure as Python dataclasses and train models to generate typed code;
REBEL~\cite{cabot2021rebel}, InstructUIE~\cite{wang2023instructuie}, DeepStruct~\cite{wang2022deepstruct}, UIE~\cite{lu2022uie}, USM~\cite{lou2023usm}, and UniversalNER~\cite{zhou2024universalner} unify extraction via structured training, though schema compliance gaps persist~\cite{wadhwa2023revisiting}.
These methods internalize constraints through training; code-generation approaches such as GoLLIE achieve type compliance through format constraints (class names encode types) but produce 45\% empty outputs on zero-shot RE (vs.\ 0\% for OntoCoDec), reflecting a coverage--compliance trade-off.
OntoCoDec enforces types at decoding time without retraining while preserving extraction coverage.

\paragraph{Constraint enforcement in IE.}
\citet{roth_yih_2004} first formulated hard type constraints for IE via integer linear programming; OntoCoDec achieves analogous enforcement within autoregressive decoding.
Post-hoc validation~\cite{khorshidi2025odke,spires_2024,ontologx_2025,slot2025} detects violations after generation and requires rejection or correction cycles.
EnriCo~\cite{zaratiana2024enrico} enforces structural constraints via ASP but requires hand-crafted rules; IterGen~\cite{ugare2025itergen} supports semantic constraints via backtracking but requires manual implementation per constraint.
BoostCD~\cite{boostcd2025} combines constrained and unconstrained decoding for IE; SchemaRL~\cite{schema_rl2025} uses reinforcement learning to align generation with schema constraints; DCCD~\cite{dccd2026} accelerates constrained decoding via draft-conditioned generation.
Recent work shows constrained decoding can degrade reasoning~\cite{banerjee2025crane,schall2025hiddencost,formattax2026}; however, extraction tasks are robust to format constraints~\cite{tam2024letmespeak}, and OntoCoDec constrains only type tokens while leaving entity spans unconstrained.
OntoCoDec prevents violations during decoding, requires no constraint-specific training, and compiles constraints automatically from IE ontologies.

% Section 7 — Discussion and Conclusion
% Full discussion in Appendix; Mistral boundary condition in app:dual-factor.

OntoCoDec formally compiles IE ontologies into composable token-level constraints via a decidability-guided architecture: LoRA + greedy S1 achieves DR\,$\leq$\,0.20\%, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% for calibrated models.
Constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) characterizes the dataset-level constraint regime; per-relation analysis reveals entity type confusability as the critical co-factor (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}), and post-hoc type resolution complements S1 on low-$\bar{\kappa}$ schemas (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}).
The decidability taxonomy and $\bar{\kappa}$ diagnostic together provide a principled workflow for deploying type-safe IE: classify constraints, compile enforcement layers, and select decoding strategy by schema tightness.
Future directions include entity-level type consensus for CF resolution during decoding, streaming inference optimization, and integration with schema-encoding training approaches.

\label{sec:wikievents}

We apply OntoCoDec to event extraction (EE) on WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} (56 event types, 80 roles, 27 entity types, 245 constraints; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents}) without modification.

\paragraph{Results.}
Unconstrained EE produces extreme vocabulary violations (EV+RoV $>$85\%; Table~\ref{tab:wikievents}), with entity F1\,=\,0 because the parser cannot process off-schema output.
Full S1 eliminates EV and RoV across all models, which validates the tokenizer-agnostic design across byte-level BPE and SentencePiece.
Grammar-only eliminates EV but leaves RoV at 64--77\% and surfaces latent AC (8--14\%), consistent with DocRED's pattern (\S\ref{sec:docred-results}); full S1 drives RoV to 0\%.
Residual AC (1.3--3.8\%) traces to semantically similar types (e.g., SID vs.\ SEN).
CF rises to 15--21\%, exceeding RE levels (10--12\%) because EE's multi-argument structures increase entity reuse across slots.
Post-hoc filtering is impractical ($<$0.5\% arguments retained).
Unlike RE, EE shows measurable F1 gains: entity F1 0\%\,$\to$\,12--18\%, trigger F1 $+$1.5--1.8\,pp.

% exp_ids: p1_ee_ft_qwen_wikievents_r5, p1_ee_ft_llama_wikievents_r5
\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning (preliminary).}
WikiEvents uses a 194/20/20 train/dev/test split~\cite{li2021document}; the 20-document test set is a dataset constraint, not a design choice.
LoRA + S1 eliminates RoV (Qwen 38.31\%\,$\to$\,0\%, Llama 8.8\%\,$\to$\,0\%; bootstrap 95\% CI [0\%,\,0\%] and [0\%,\,1.73\%]) and reduces AC to $\leq$0.8\%, with argument F1 within $\pm$1.1\,pp; trigger F1 shows larger shifts ($-$5.4/$-$0.6\,pp) with wide confidence intervals at this sample size.
CF remains low under fine-tuning (0.77--1.18\%), consistent with RE composability results (\S\ref{sec:composition}, Table~\ref{tab:composability}).
Constrained decoding does not further reduce EE CF because the semantic layer enforces per-event role-type compatibility but not cross-event entity type consensus, the same architectural limitation identified in RE (\S\ref{sec:composition}).

3	\section{Introduction}
4	\label{sec:introduction}
5	
6	Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
7	We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
8	Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
9	Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
10	At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.
11	
12	Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
13	Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
14	Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
15	Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
16	OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from any IE ontology.
    \item An analytical framework for constraint behavior: constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) characterizes the dataset-level constraint regime across 103 relations and determines post-hoc resolution feasibility (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); four violation categories (DR, RV, ET, CF) decompose the violation landscape.
    \item Cross-configuration validation: LoRA + greedy S1 achieves DR$\to$0\% with R-F1 $\pm$0.6\,pp, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% across 8B--70B models. The framework extends to event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.

%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.

% Section 1: Introduction (compressed, 669→~550 words)

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Large language models are increasingly used for information extraction~\cite{li2023codeie,sainz2024gollie,wei2023zeroshot}, but when generating relation triples $(h, r, t)$, neither entity is guaranteed to carry a type consistent with the ontology's domain/range constraints for $r$.
We call such outputs \emph{domain/range violations}: structurally valid triples that are ontologically invalid.
Violations persist across the capability spectrum: 15.4\% of triples on SciERC~\cite{luan2018scierc} and 18.5\% on DocRED~\cite{yao2019docred} under zero-shot decoding, and 1--2\% even after LoRA fine-tuning; rates correlate with \emph{constraint tightness} (few valid type pairs per relation) rather than ontology or model scale.
Type violations are ontologically invalid regardless of downstream application: a triple whose head or tail type lies outside the relation's domain/range specification contradicts the schema definition.
At deployment-grade quality (R-F1 40--46\%), where extracted triples feed directly into knowledge graphs, reliable type-safety enforcement is needed.

Existing approaches leave a fundamental gap.
Schema-informed prompting reduces violations by 62\% on average but is per-relation unreliable (violations for \textsc{Evaluate-for} actually \emph{increase} by 5.8\,pp).
Grammar-constrained decoding~\cite{dong2025xgrammar,willard2023outlines,beurer-kellner2023lmql} guarantees syntactic well-formedness but cannot encode cross-field semantic constraints.
Post-hoc filtering achieves higher F1 in most zero-shot settings via precision gains, but at the cost of discarding up to 48\% of predictions including true positives; at high rejection rates (e.g., Mistral DocRED 73.7\%), it discards the majority of outputs and becomes impractical.
OntoCoDec preserves recall by enforcing constraints during generation rather than discarding non-compliant outputs.
Training-based approaches~\cite{sainz2024gollie,lu2022uie} provide only soft guidance that cannot eliminate violations.

We propose \textbf{OntoCoDec}, a framework that formally compiles IE ontologies into composable layers of decoding-time constraints.
A decidability analysis of IE type constraints (\S\ref{sec:decidability}) yields a two-layer architecture: the \emph{grammar layer} enforces context-free constraints (JSON structure, vocabulary membership) via XGrammar; the \emph{semantic layer} enforces prefix-decidable constraints (pair-based domain/range) through dynamic logit masking over a runtime entity registry, with an \emph{enabling dependency} between layers.
OntoCoDec compiles constraints automatically from any IE ontology, requires no constraint-specific training, and applies to any autoregressive LM.
We evaluate two deployment configurations: LoRA + greedy S1 eliminates DR with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp and $+$10\% latency; LoRA + beam S1 ($k{=}4$) additionally resolves the CF trade-off, achieving zero violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency).
Zero-shot evaluation across four models (8B--70B) confirms DR drops by 76--99\% for calibrated models.

Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,itemsep=2pt]
    \item A formal ontology-to-constraint compilation framework: we classify IE type constraints by decidability (context-free, prefix-decidable with state, non-local), yielding a two-layer architecture with pair-based sequential enforcement and formal guarantees at each level (\S\ref{sec:decidability}). Constraints compile automatically from any IE ontology.
    \item An analytical framework for constraint behavior: constraint tightness ($\bar{\kappa}$) characterizes the dataset-level constraint regime across 103 relations and determines post-hoc resolution feasibility (Appendix~\ref{app:tcr}); four violation categories (DR, RV, ET, CF) decompose the violation landscape.
    \item Cross-configuration validation: LoRA + greedy S1 achieves DR$\to$0\% with R-F1 $\pm$0.6\,pp, CF\,$\leq$\,1.2\%; beam ($k{=}4$) eliminates all violations on SciERC (1.54$\times$ latency); zero-shot DR drops 76--99\% across 8B--70B models. The framework extends to event extraction (\S\ref{sec:wikievents}).
\end{enumerate}

% Section: Constraint Composition (compressed, 787→~500 words)

At each decoding step $t$, let $G(t) \subseteq V$ and $S(t) \subseteq V$ denote the tokens permitted by the grammar and semantic layers, respectively.
The final mask is their conjunction:
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:composition}
  M_{\text{final}}(t) = M_{\text{grammar}}(t) \;\wedge\; M_{\text{semantic}}(t),
\end{equation}
%
so a token is allowed only if it satisfies \emph{both} structural and type-level constraints.
The conjunction is asymmetric: $S(t)$ is defined only over $G(t)$. This reflects the enabling dependency (\S\ref{sec:method}): the semantic layer requires the relation type to belong to $\mathcal{R}$, a property guaranteed only by the grammar layer.

\paragraph{Grammar-First Fallback.}
When $S(t) \cap G(t) = \emptyset$ (tight constraints leave no token that is both grammar-valid and semantically valid), na\"{\i}ve masking would force selection of a grammar-invalid token, breaking JSON structure.
We enforce a \emph{grammar-first fallback}: if no semantically valid token survives grammar filtering, semantic masking is skipped and the grammar layer alone controls selection.
Structural integrity is a hard constraint; a type violation is a soft error detectable by downstream validation.
Among type violations, DR and CF differ in severity: a DR violation renders the triple ontologically invalid (the entity type lies outside the relation's domain or range), whereas a CF violation means each triple is individually schema-valid but the same entity receives different type assignments across triples.

\paragraph{Constraint Tightness.}
Recall the tightness of relation $r$ (\S\ref{sec:bg:ontology}):\footnote{For symmetric relations, $|\sigma(r)|$ counts ordered pairs; the normalization $|\mathcal{E}|^2$ remains appropriate since we evaluate on directed triples.}
%
\begin{equation}\label{eq:tightness}
  \kappa(r) = 1 - \frac{|\sigma(r)|}{|\mathcal{E}|^2},
\end{equation}
%
The mean tightness $\bar{\kappa} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}|}\sum_{r} \kappa(r)$ characterizes schema restrictiveness.
Tighter constraints eliminate more grammar-valid tokens at type-bearing positions; fallback frequency and residual DR increase accordingly.
This dual-factor pattern (tightness $\times$ baseline violation rate; $n{=}4$ model--dataset pairs, descriptive) aligns with the cross-dataset results: SciERC ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.333$) achieves 94--99\% DR reduction vs.\ DocRED ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.842$) at 45--90\%; the full range across three models is 42--99\% (\S\ref{sec:cross-model}; Appendix~\ref{app:dual-factor}).
The pattern extends to WikiEvents EE ($\bar{\kappa}{=}0.82$; Appendix~\ref{app:wikievents-kappa}).
However, $\kappa$ is necessary but not sufficient for high violation rates: per-relation analysis shows that high-$\kappa$ relations with unambiguous entity types (\textsc{place\_of\_birth}, $\kappa{=}0.92$, DR${=}$0\%) have zero violations, while relations with comparable $\kappa$ but confusable types (\textsc{basin\_country}, $\kappa{=}0.97$, DR${=}$74.6\%) are highly vulnerable (Appendix~\ref{app:kappa-case-study}).
$\bar{\kappa}$ provides deployment guidance: schemas with $\bar{\kappa} < 0.5$ achieve near-complete DR elimination under zero-shot S1 (94--99\% reduction); schemas with $\bar{\kappa} > 0.8$ require fine-tuning to narrow the fallback regime (DR\,0.01--0.20\%).

\paragraph{Non-Rectangularity and Sequential Masking.}
\label{sec:rectangularity}
% Data source: artifacts/rebuttal/w2_rectangularity_report.md
Sequential masking is necessary because ontology type signatures are non-rectangular (0/7 SciERC, 23/96 DocRED relations satisfy $\sigma(r) = \operatorname{dom}(r) \times \operatorname{range}(r)$); independent enforcement would admit 33--37\% spurious pairs.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Fine-tuning narrows the fallback regime: DR drops to $\leq$\,0.20\% and CF to $\leq$\,1.18\%, with R-F1 within $\pm$0.6\,pp; the grammar layer becomes a no-op and the semantic layer alone reduces residual DR by 39--72\% (\S\ref{sec:composability}).
